strengths: Novel and elegant technical contributions: The causal decomposition (Theorem 2.5) factorizing observable operators into world-channel and adversary-aggregation components is a key innovation. The reference posterior-predictive formulation (Definition 2.2) elegantly avoids circularity issues present in concurrent work.

Complete theoretical characterization: Matching upper bound Õ(H√(β̄_T d_E T) + mH log T) and lower bound Ω(√(d_E T)) establish minimax optimality (with caveats). Explicit dependence on all problem parameters (H, m, d_E, β_T) is clean and interpretable.

Principled algorithmic design: One-policy-per-epoch with geometric caps and statistical termination is well-justified. Proposition D.5 proves termination is necessary, showing fixed schedules suffer Ω(T) regret. Cumulative confidence sets enable efficient information aggregation.

Important problem formulation: Policy regret against memory-bounded adaptive adversaries in partially observable settings is fundamental for multi-agent RL and well-motivated (autonomous vehicles, trading, security).

High technical quality: Careful handling of data-dependent epoch lengths with proper union bounds, novel Eluder dimension analysis via channel decomposition, and rigorous concentration arguments throughout.

Comprehensive treatment: Multiple extensions (adaptive horizon Theorem 5.1, fading memory Theorem 5.2, tabular bounds Theorem 5.3), empirical validation confirming theoretical predictions, detailed comparison with concurrent work.
weaknesses: Computational intractability: Optimistic planning requires solving max_{(π,ξ)∈Π×C} V^π(ξ), which is PSPACE-complete even with known parameters. Section 5.4 acknowledges but doesn't resolve this, severely limiting practical applicability beyond toy problems (Bernoulli bandits).

Lower bound generality gap: Lower bound uses H=2, fully revealing observations, and memoryless adversary, while upper bound handles general H, partial observability, and m-memory adversaries. Optimality claim is incomplete—matching lower bounds for the full problem generality are missing.

Avoidable H factor in confidence radius: β̄_T = Hβ_T seems to include an unnecessary H factor. Remark D.13 suggests aggregate KL conversion could eliminate this, but it's not used in main result. For tabular settings this compounds to Θ(H²) terms.

Structural assumptions insufficiently motivated: Posterior-Lipschitz (Assumption 2.3) and weak revealing (Assumption 2.4) are stated but lack sufficient justification. Beyond Remark D.1, few examples of when posterior-Lipschitz holds. The uniform requirement over θ ∈ Θ appears restrictive.

Limited novelty in algorithmic components: Optimistic MLE framework from Liu et al. (2023), Eluder dimension from Russo & Van Roy (2013), epoch structure inspired by low-switching RL. Main novelty is combining these with causal decomposition—meaningful but somewhat incremental.

Experimental validation is limited: Experiments 1-2 only work for Bernoulli bandits where MLE is tractable. Experiment 3 uses simplified/simulated adversary on real data. No comparison with alternative approaches (posterior sampling, other RL methods). No demonstration on problems where partial observability or adversarial response is essential.

Presentation and technical clarity: Heavy notation with superscripts/subscripts makes sections difficult to parse. Distinction between full augmented space S̄⁺ and reduced space S̄⁺_red introduced late. Sign-witness lemma (Lemma C.1) is dense. Paper exceeds 40 pages with potentially condensable appendix content.
